Early Tongan chiefdoms.name: Early Tongan chiefdoms
Early Tongan chiefdoms.description: Lapita voyagers reached Tongatapu around 880–850 BCE, among the first people in Polynesia. Over the next two millennia Ancestral Polynesian culture took shape here and in Samoa.

Tuʻi Tonga Empire.name: Tuʻi Tonga Empire
Tuʻi Tonga Empire.description: Founded c. 950 by ʻAhoʻeitu, the first Tuʻi Tonga. Ruled from Muʻa on Tongatapu with a fleet of double-hulled kalia canoes. Power later passed to the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua and Tuʻi Kanokupolu lines; civil wars from 1799 ended with unification under Tāufaʻāhau (George Tupou I).

(Tuʻi Tonga Empire).name: Tuʻi Tonga Empire
(Tuʻi Tonga Empire).description: At its height (c. 1200–1500) Tongan power and tribute networks reached ʻUvea, Futuna, Niue, the Lau Islands of Fiji and, through war and marriage alliances, Samoa. Drawn as a sphere of influence rather than a fixed border.

Kingdom of Tonga.name: Kingdom of Tonga
Kingdom of Tonga.description: Unified by George Tupou I in 1845, with a constitution in 1875. A British protected state from 1900 to 1970, but never colonised — the only Pacific kingdom to keep its monarchy throughout.

Samoan chiefdoms.name: Samoan chiefdoms
Samoan chiefdoms.description: Settled by c. 800 BCE (Lapita pottery at Mulifanua). Ruled through the matai chiefly system and paramount titles. Tradition tells of Tongan occupation c. 950–1250, ended by the brothers Tuna and Fata and the rise of the Malietoa title; Salamasina became the first to hold all four paramount titles c. 1500. Rival claimants backed by Germany, Britain and the US fought civil wars in 1886–1899, ending in partition.

German Samoa.name: German Samoa
German Samoa.description: Western Samoa became a German protectorate under the 1899 Tripartite Convention. The Mau resistance movement began under German rule.

Western Samoa (New Zealand).name: Western Samoa (New Zealand)
Western Samoa (New Zealand).description: Occupied by New Zealand in 1914. The Mau movement for independence grew after the 1918 influenza disaster and 'Black Saturday' in 1929.

Samoa.name: Samoa
Samoa.description: The first Pacific nation to regain independence, in 1962.

American Samoa.name: American Samoa
American Samoa.description: Tutuila and Manuʻa were ceded to the United States in 1900 and 1904.

Niuean chiefdoms.name: Niuean chiefdoms
Niuean chiefdoms.description: Settled from Samoa and later Tonga, perhaps around 900 CE. Niue had paramount kings (patuiki) from the 18th century and resisted outside contact; it became a British protectorate in 1900.

Fijian chiefdoms.name: Fijian chiefdoms
Fijian chiefdoms.description: Settled by Lapita voyagers c. 1000 BCE. Fiji's warring chiefdoms (matanitu) such as Bau, Rewa, Verata and Cakaudrove were closely tied to Tonga; Tongan prince Enele Maʻafu dominated the Lau Islands in the 1850s–60s before Seru Epenisa Cakobau proclaimed a Kingdom of Fiji.

Colony of Fiji.name: Colony of Fiji
Colony of Fiji.description: Cakobau ceded Fiji to Britain in 1874. Independence followed in 1970.

Hawaiʻi Island chiefdom.name: Hawaiʻi Island chiefdom
Hawaiʻi Island chiefdom.description: Polynesian voyagers reached Hawaiʻi roughly 1000–1200 CE. Hawaiʻi Island was unified under ʻUmi-a-Līloa (c. 1500); its aliʻi nui waged repeated wars on Maui. Kamehameha won the island after his last rival there, Keōua Kūʻahuʻula, was killed at Puʻukoholā Heiau in 1791.

Maui chiefdom.name: Maui chiefdom
Maui chiefdom.description: Maui's chiefs, among them Piʻilani (c. 1500) who built the King's Highway, contested Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi and fought Hawaiʻi Island for centuries.

Maui chiefdom under Kahekili II.name: Maui chiefdom under Kahekili II
Maui chiefdom under Kahekili II.description: Kahekili II conquered Oʻahu in 1783 and ruled Maui, Oʻahu, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi — the strongest rival to Kamehameha until his death in 1794.

Oʻahu chiefdom.name: Oʻahu chiefdom
Oʻahu chiefdom.description: Oʻahu's ruling line (Kākuhihewa, Kūaliʻi and others) held the island until Kahekili II of Maui conquered it in 1783.

Kauaʻi chiefdom.name: Kauaʻi chiefdom
Kauaʻi chiefdom.description: Kauaʻi and Niʻihau were never conquered: Kamehameha's invasion fleets of 1796 and 1804 failed (storm and epidemic). King Kaumualiʻi accepted Kamehameha's overlordship peacefully in 1810.

Society Islands chiefdoms.name: Society Islands chiefdoms
Society Islands chiefdoms.description: Settled around 1000 CE, a launching point for voyages to Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa and Rapa Nui. Taputapuātea marae on Raiatea was the religious centre of eastern Polynesia; the ʻarioi society travelled between islands.

Kingdom of Tahiti.name: Kingdom of Tahiti
Kingdom of Tahiti.description: Pōmare I unified Tahiti using European muskets and allies from the Bounty mutineers. Queen Pōmare IV ruled 1827–1877; France imposed a protectorate in 1842, which Tahitians resisted in the Franco-Tahitian War (1844–1847), and annexed the kingdom in 1880.

Marquesan chiefdoms.name: Marquesan chiefdoms
Marquesan chiefdoms.description: Settled c. 1000 CE or earlier; a hub of East Polynesian voyaging. Valleys were ruled by rival tribal chiefs. France annexed the islands in 1842.

French Oceania.name: French Oceania
French Oceania.description: France annexed the Marquesas in 1842, the first step in building French Oceania.

French Polynesia.name: French Polynesia
French Polynesia.description: An overseas collectivity of France since 1946 (renamed 1957).

Cook Islands chiefdoms.name: Cook Islands chiefdoms
Cook Islands chiefdoms.description: Settled from the Society Islands around 1000 CE. Rarotonga was divided among ariki (high chiefs) of the Makea, Pa and Kainuku lines. Tradition names Rarotonga as a departure point for voyages to Aotearoa.

Cook Islands.name: Cook Islands
Cook Islands.description: A British protectorate from 1888, annexed to New Zealand in 1901, self-governing in free association with New Zealand since 1965.

Rapa Nui.name: Rapa Nui
Rapa Nui.description: The easternmost reach of Polynesian voyaging, settled c. 1200. Rapa Nui's clans carved nearly a thousand moai. From around 1760 the Tangata manu (birdman) contest at Orongo chose the island's leader. Peruvian slave raids in 1862 and epidemics devastated the population; Chile annexed the island in 1888.

Moriori.name: Moriori
Moriori.description: Polynesians who settled Rēkohu (the Chatham Islands) from Aotearoa around 1500 and developed a distinct culture. Under Nunuku-whenua's law they renounced war. In 1835 Māori of Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama invaded and enslaved them.

Colony of New Zealand.name: Colony of New Zealand
Colony of New Zealand.description: Proclaimed after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). British sovereignty was contested across much of the North Island through the New Zealand Wars (1845–1872), and Māori held the King Country until the 1880s.

Dominion of New Zealand.name: Dominion of New Zealand
Dominion of New Zealand.description: Self-governing dominion of the British Empire until full independence in 1947.

Kingdom of Mapungubwe.name: Kingdom of Mapungubwe
Kingdom of Mapungubwe.description: The first class-divided state in southern Africa, centred on Mapungubwe Hill at the Limpopo–Shashe confluence. Traded gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean; famous for its golden rhinoceros. Its decline preceded the rise of Great Zimbabwe.

Kingdom of Butua (Torwa).name: Kingdom of Butua (Torwa)
Kingdom of Butua (Torwa).description: The Torwa dynasty ruled south-western Zimbabwe from Khami after Great Zimbabwe declined, rivalling Mutapa. It was absorbed into Changamire Dombo's Rozvi state in the 1680s.

Mthethwa Paramountcy.name: Mthethwa Paramountcy
Mthethwa Paramountcy.description: Under Dingiswayo, the Mthethwa built a confederacy of northern Nguni chiefdoms and reorganised its army into age regiments. Shaka served as one of his commanders. Dingiswayo's death at the hands of Zwide in 1817/18 opened the way for the Zulu.

Ndwandwe.name: Ndwandwe
Ndwandwe.description: Zwide's Ndwandwe were the great rival of the Mthethwa and then the Zulu. Shaka defeated them at the Mhlatuze River in 1819; Ndwandwe fugitives under Soshangane, Zwangendaba and others carried the Mfecane north as far as Lake Victoria.

Kingdom of Eswatini (Ngwane).name: Kingdom of Eswatini (Ngwane)
Kingdom of Eswatini (Ngwane).description: The Dlamini kings led the Ngwane north to the Pongola and then into modern Eswatini. Sobhuza I avoided destruction in the Mfecane through diplomacy and strategic retreat; Mswati II made the Swazi a major regional power.

Ife.name: Ife
Ife.description: The sacred city-state of the Yoruba, whose naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads (12th–15th centuries) are among Africa's great artworks. Yoruba kings, including the Alaafin of Oyo, traced their authority to Ife's first ruler, Oduduwa.

Ndebele Kingdom.name: Ndebele Kingdom
Ndebele Kingdom.description: Mthwakazi under Mzilikazi and then Lobengula, after settling around Bulawayo c. 1840. Borders drawn from the 1878 map.

Kingdom of Zimbabwe.name: Kingdom of Zimbabwe
Kingdom of Zimbabwe.description: Builders of Great Zimbabwe, the largest stone ruins south of the Sahara. A Shona state that grew rich on gold and ivory traded to the Swahili coast, at its height c. 1220–1450.

Māori iwi.name: Māori iwi
Māori iwi.description: Polynesian voyagers settled Aotearoa around 1280 and formed iwi (tribes) and hapū led by rangatira. Inter-iwi warfare intensified with muskets in the Musket Wars (1807–1842).

Kingdom of Benin.name: Kingdom of Benin
Kingdom of Benin.description: Ruled by the Obas from Benin City, with a disciplined army that subjugated hundreds of towns. Famous for its bronze plaques, looted in the British punitive expedition of 1897.

Kingdom of Mutapa.name: Kingdom of Mutapa
Kingdom of Mutapa.description: Founded c. 1430 by Nyatsimba Mutota after the decline of Great Zimbabwe. Mutapa conquered the land between the Zambezi and Limpopo and controlled gold trade with the Swahili and later the Portuguese, who made it a vassal in 1629.

Rozvi Empire.name: Rozvi Empire
Rozvi Empire.description: Founded by Changamire Dombo, who broke from Mutapa and drove the Portuguese from the Zimbabwean plateau in the 1690s. A professional, hierarchical army collected cattle as tribute. It fell to Nguni invaders during the Mfecane in the 1830s.

Zulu Kingdom.name: Zulu Kingdom
Zulu Kingdom.description: Shaka transformed a small clan into a conquest state after 1816, with the short stabbing spear, large shields and the 'buffalo horns' formation. His wars set off the Mfecane across southern Africa. The kingdom defeated the British at Isandlwana (1879) before falling to them later that year.
